subject: Chemistry
description: Monomers, addition vs condensation, thermoplastic vs thermoset, common polymers + uses

questions.stem: A polymer is best described as:

options.option_text: A large molecule built from repeating subunits called monomers

questions.explanation: Polymer (Greek 'poly' many + 'mer' parts) — long chains/networks of repeating monomer units. Natural polymers — cellulose (glucose monomers), starch, proteins (amino acid monomers), DNA (nucleotides), rubber (isoprene). Synthetic polymers — polyethylene (ethylene), PVC (vinyl chloride), nylon, Teflon, polyester, Bakelite. Two formation reactions — Addition polymerisation (monomers add directly, no byproduct) and Condensation polymerisation (loses small molecules like water).

questions.explanation: Polythene / Polyethylene — repeating −CH₂−CH₂− units made from ethylene C₂H₄ via addition polymerisation. World's most widely produced plastic. Two main types: LDPE (Low Density, ~0.92 g/cm³, branched, used in plastic bags, films) and HDPE (High Density, ~0.96 g/cm³, linear, used in milk jugs, pipes, hard hats). PVC = polyvinyl chloride (from vinyl chloride CH₂=CHCl). PVA = polyvinyl acetate. PS = polystyrene (from styrene C₆H₅CH=CH₂).

questions.stem: Bakelite — the world's first synthetic plastic (1907) — is a:

options.option_text: Thermosetting plastic (cannot be remelted once cured)

questions.explanation: Bakelite — Leo Baekeland (1907) — phenol-formaldehyde resin. Thermoset: once cured, it cannot be remelted (cross-linked 3D network). Used in electrical switches, plug sockets, telephone handsets, kitchen utensils, billiard balls. Other thermosets: Melamine, Urea-formaldehyde, Epoxy, Polyurethane (some). Thermoplastics — soften on heating, can be remoulded (PE, PVC, PS, PP, nylon, acrylic). Elastomers — stretchy (rubber, silicone, neoprene).

questions.stem: Teflon — known for non-stick cookware coatings — is chemically:
questions.explanation: Teflon — DuPont brand for PTFE, accidentally discovered 1938 by Roy Plunkett. C-F bond is one of the strongest in chemistry → PTFE is chemically inert, slippery, withstands −240 to +260 °C. Used in cookware (since 1960s), gaskets, plumbing tape, expedition clothing (Gore-Tex laminate), wire insulation. Concerns about PFOA/PFAS additives (forever chemicals); newer products are PFOA-free.

questions.stem: Nylon-6,6 is formed by condensation polymerisation of:

options.option_text: Hexamethylenediamine + Adipic acid (each contributing 6 carbons → name nylon 6,6)

questions.explanation: Nylon-6,6 — Wallace Carothers (DuPont, 1935). Condensation polymerisation between hexamethylenediamine (H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂, 6 carbons) and adipic acid (HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH, 6 carbons → 4 carbons + 2 COOH-C = 6) — hence '6,6'. Forms amide linkages (-CO-NH-) like proteins. Loses water as byproduct. Strong, lightweight, stockings, parachutes, ropes. Nylon-6 is from caprolactam (just one monomer, ring-opening polymerisation).

questions.stem: PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate), used in soft-drink bottles, has the recycling identifier number:
questions.explanation: Resin Identification Codes (1-7, used worldwide): 1 = PET / PETE (water bottles, soda bottles, polyester fibres); 2 = HDPE (milk jugs, shampoo); 3 = PVC (pipes, vinyl); 4 = LDPE (grocery bags); 5 = PP (yoghurt cups, bottle caps); 6 = PS (foam cups, packing peanuts); 7 = OTHER (bioplastics, polycarbonates, mixed). Lower numbers (1, 2, 5) generally most recyclable. PET is also used as polyester fibres in clothing.

questions.stem: Natural rubber is a polymer of which monomer?
questions.explanation: Natural rubber — cis-1,4-polyisoprene, from the latex of Hevea brasiliensis tree (Pará rubber, Brazil origin). Vulcanisation (Charles Goodyear, 1839) — heat with sulphur → cross-links → improves elasticity, durability, heat resistance — basis of tyres. Synthetic rubbers — Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR, in tyres), Polybutadiene, Neoprene (chloroprene), Buna-S, Buna-N. Largest natural-rubber producer — Thailand; India is one of the top 5 (Kerala accounts for 90% of India's production).
